Female Cocoa snapper reach a maximum fork length of 50 cm [Li = 50 cm], a size that places them among the more moderately sized lutjanids inhabiting the mesophotic reefs of the southwestern Pacific. This ultimate length corresponds to an asymptotic body mass of 2754 grams [Wwi = 2754 grams], a figure that reflects the energetic constraints of their deep reef habitat. In comparison to closely related snappers within the genus Paracaesio, this ultimate mass is consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritizes gradual somatic growth over rapid early maturation, a pattern commonly observed in species that occupy stable, low-productivity environments.

The onset of reproductive capability in female Cocoa snapper is marked by a fork length of 40 cm [Lp = 40 cm], corresponding to a wet weight at puberty of 1445 grams [Wwp = 1445 grams]. Achieving this body mass represents a significant energetic investment, and individuals typically require several years of sustained feeding before reaching this threshold. The maturation schedule appears to be tightly linked to the attainment of a critical body size rather than a fixed age, a characteristic that buffers the population against interannual variability in food availability. This size-based threshold ensures that females have accumulated sufficient energy reserves to support the high metabolic demands of vitellogenesis and spawning, while postponing reproductive effort until somatic growth is well advanced.

At the earliest stage of life, individual Cocoa snapper emerge from small pelagic eggs with a calculated wet weight of 0.00032 grams [Wwb = 0.00032 grams]. This minute birth mass underscores the extreme vulnerability of the early larval phase. The yolk-sac larva that hatches from such an egg is entirely lecithotrophic, relying on endogenous yolk reserves to sustain development during the first few days post-hatching. The transition to exogenous feeding represents a critical bottleneck, as the tiny gape size of the newly hatched larva restricts initial prey to the smallest size fractions of the zooplankton community. The low initial mass also implies a high mass-specific metabolic rate, which, when combined with the limited yolk energy, constrains the duration of the non-feeding period and sets a narrow window for successful first feeding.

The maximum daily reproductive output of a mature female Cocoa snapper has been estimated by scaling the fecundity of the related stripey snapper Lutjanus carponotatus to the larger body size of Paracaesio stonei. Under a stable thermal regime of 19.2 °C [T = 19.2 °C], this species is estimated to release 749,000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = 749,000 eggs per spawning event], with approximately 3 spawning events occurring per year [F_R_i = approximately 3 spawning events occurring per year]. The pelagic eggs are broadcast into the water column during spawning aggregations, where fertilization is external and the developing embryos drift with ocean currents. This high fecundity, typical of tropical lutjanids, compensates for the extremely low survival probability of each individual egg through the planktonic larval phase.

Longevity records for the Cocoa snapper, based on otolith annuli from a population sampled at a mean annual temperature of 19.2 °C [T = 19.2 °C], indicate a maximum lifespan of 20 years [am = 20 years]. This extended lifespan, approaching two decades, aligns with the species' late maturation and large ultimate body size, fitting a classic slow-rebound life-history syndrome common among deep-reef lutjanids. The oldest individuals in the sample exhibited clear signs of reproductive senescence, with a marked reduction in gonadosomatic index among females beyond 16 years of age. This age-related decline in reproductive output suggests that the species relies on a prolonged adult survival phase to offset the high early-life mortality inherent to its pelagic larval strategy.
